headline: Licensing, Insurance, and Permits for Bathroom Remodeling in Los Angeles County
articleBody: Homeowners in Los Angeles County should begin by verifying that any bathroom remodeling contractor holds an active California contractor’s license in the appropriate classification, typically **B – General Building** or **C‑36 – Plumbing** for plumbing‑intensive work. The California Contractors State License Board (CSLB), a state regulatory agency, provides a public online license lookup that shows license status, bond, workers’ compensation coverage, and any disciplinary actions. CSLB guidance emphasizes that contracts for home improvement work over $500 in labor and materials require a licensed contractor and written contract. Insurance verification is equally important. Industry best practice, reflected in construction trade association guidance, recommends asking for proof of **general liability insurance** and **workers’ compensation**. The liability policy helps cover property damage or certain third‑party injuries arising from the work, while workers’ compensation protects workers and insulates the homeowner from potential injury claims. Homeowners should request certificates issued by the insurer rather than relying on contractor statements. In Los Angeles County, bathroom renovations that involve moving walls, altering structural elements, adding new plumbing lines, changing electrical circuits, or modifying ventilation typically require permits and inspections under local building and residential codes. The Los Angeles Department of Building and Safety (LADBS) explains that the **permit holder is normally the contractor**, not the homeowner, and inspections must be passed before final sign‑off. Building officials and national model codes (such as the International Residential Code and California Building Code) stress that permitted work helps ensure compliance with life‑safety, structural, plumbing, and electrical standards. Consumers should avoid contractors who propose doing the job “without permits” to save money or who ask the homeowner to pull an owner‑builder permit while they act as an unlicensed builder. CSLB and consumer protection agencies warn that such arrangements can shift liability, code compliance responsibility, and employment law risks onto the homeowner in ways many do not anticipate.
